newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinese troops brave Hong Kong's traffic maze.
newsitem.headline: Chinese troops brave Hong Kong's traffic maze.

text.p: Advance troops from China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) arrived in capitalist Hong Kong on Monday to find themselves immediately fighting the traffic and maze of interchanges.

But few Hong Kong people paid much attention as the 40-member party of mainland troops wound through the territory's streets and pulled into the barracks housing the British forces in the heart of the business quarter.
"What is there to fear?" said a middle-aged woman waiting to catch a glimpse of the PLA convoy near the Prince of Wales barracks on the Hong Kong waterfront.

The eight-vehicle convoy of black saloon cars, coaches and camouflage-painted lorries cleared customs at the rural Lok Ma Chau crossing and made the 30 km (20 mile) drive from the border escorted by local traffic police as the drivers grappled with the switch to driving on the left side of the road.
Inside, the Chinese soldiers sat bolt-upright and looked straight ahead as Hong Kong flashed past. Some stole quick sideways glances and others gave an occasional smile.
British soldiers serving as guides in each vehicle were as expressionless as their Chinese counterparts.
The PLA takes over the defence of Hong Kong when Britain lowers the Union Jack at midnight on June 30 and hands back the territory to communist China after more than 150 years of colonial rule.
The unarmed advance party -- the first members of a garrison which could eventually number up to 10,000 -- is in Hong Kong to set up military facilities.
Small pockets of Hong Kong people waited at strategic points alone the route for a glimpse of the convoy.
A dozen waved from a bridge. A handful more took up positions near the entrance to the Lion Rock Tunnel, which connects the New Territories with Hong Kong island's urban congestion.
Cameras flashed but overall interest on the streets of Hong Kong was muted.

A doctor walking through the bustling Central business district with his family said the PLA's arrival was "nothing exciting" and that life in Hong Kong would carry on as usual after the full garrison arrives.
"It will stay the way it is. It will be okay," he said. "I'm not paying too much attention."
Earlier in the day, Democratic Party leader Martin Lee painted a different picture.

"The stationing of troops in Shenzhen (over the border in China) would have been sufficient to protect Hong Kong if necessary," Lee told a news conference after returning from a three-week lobbying tour of Europe and North America.
"...I don't think Hong Kong people will feel too happy about the stationing of the troops."
